newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-QUIET AMERICAN LOOKS FOR FIRST MAJOR.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-QUIET AMERICAN LOOKS FOR FIRST MAJOR.

text.p: Mark O'Meara is one of the quiet men of golf.
Apart from brief splashes of publicity when he has won a tournament, he has left it to others to grab the headlines. Until the past 12 months, that is, when he has been quoted frequently.
But many of those interviews have been not about himself but the young golfing master Tiger Woods to whom he has become a mentor.
Yet O'Meara is currently fourth in the American rankings with almost a million dollars in earnings this year and a certainty for the U.S. Ryder Cup team.

Back-to-back wins early this year, including a record fifth victory in the Pebble Beach National Pro-Am, made him only the fifth player to reach eight million dollars in career earnings on the U.S. Tour.
O'Meara has one regret. "I haven't won a professional major championship and that's a little bit disappointing," he said on Tuesday.
"But, you know, it's not from lack of effort, that's for sure. And if I could get off to a good start this week here at Troon I would hope that maybe I would have that opportunity, come Sunday."
Of the majors, the British Open which starts on Thursday is the one he is keenest to win.
"Obviously my own U.S. Open is very important but I think the British Open is the golf championship," he said.

He has come close twice before, finishing third in 1985 and 1991. On the latter occasion he was tied for the lead going into the last day and shot a 69. But Australian Ian Baker-Finch, playing the front nine "as good as I think any human being can play" fired a 66 and took the title.
O'Meara suffered a dip in form and went without a win for more than three years before two victories in 1995 and two more the following year saw him charge back up the U.S. rankings.
He admits his game has gone slightly off the boil recently. "My driving of the ball has not been that great. When your not doing that it puts a little bit more pressure on everything else."
